# Local folder source

The `local-folder` type reads a folder of documents. The first four sections
match what `okg deployment source-types` prints.

<!-- source-type:start (generated by scripts/render_source_type_pages.py) -->
## What it reads

Reads Markdown, text, JSON and YAML files under one folder, and PDF text when include names PDF files, and makes each document and its sections searchable.

Record types it adds: `document`, `document_chunk`, `entity_mention`.

## Settings

| Setting | Required | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `root` | yes |  | Folder to read (absolute path). |
| `include` | no | `["**/*.md", "**/*.txt", "**/*.json", "**/*.yaml"]` | File patterns to read. |
| `exclude` | no | `["**/.git/**", "**/node_modules/**"]` | File patterns to skip. |

## Access

No credential needed.

## Updates and removals

An edited record is detected by its content and updates the same graph record; unchanged records are left alone.
A record that is missing after a complete, successful scan is removed from the next published version. A scan that stops early or fails removes nothing.
Refreshes when you run `okg ingest --deployment <name>` or when the deployment's scheduled refresh runs; every refresh is a complete scan.
<!-- source-type:end -->

## Add it

```bash
okg deployment add-source <name> notes --type local-folder \
  --setting root=/absolute/path/to/folder
```

This previews the files it would read. Run it again with `--apply --yes` to
add the source. To read other text files, give `include` as a JSON list. The
list replaces the default, so name every pattern you want, for example
`--setting 'include=["**/*.md", "**/*.rst", "**/*.yml"]'`.

## Add PDFs

PDFs are not in the default `include`, so name them. If you forget, the
preview fails and tells you what the folder holds and the `include` to pass:

```bash
okg deployment add-source <name> papers --type local-folder \
  --setting root=/absolute/path/to/pdfs \
  --setting 'include=["**/*.pdf"]'
```

Add `--apply --yes` after the preview. Each PDF becomes a `document`, and each
page becomes a `document_chunk` whose location is `page N`. A search for a word
in the paper then returns that page.

What is read, and what is not:

- It reads the PDF's text layer, page by page. Equations and two-column pages
  come out as the PDF stores them, which can be out of reading order.
- It does not read scanned pages (images of text), figures or tables. The
  preview checks the first five pages of up to 100 PDFs and prints a warning
  when it finds none with text, or a PDF it cannot open. A scan imports as a
  record with no searchable text. Run OCR on it first, for example
  `ocrmypdf in.pdf out.pdf`, then add the folder.
- Caps stay in force: a PDF over 50 MiB (the source's `max_bytes_per_file`)
  is recorded with no text and an `oversize` warning, and the preview names
  such files without reading them. Only the first 5,000 pages of a PDF are
  read.
- A PDF that will not open, such as an encrypted one, is named in the same
  preview warning with its error class.

The packaged readers are shared. Once `extractors.yaml` carries the `pdf`
parser, any other `local-folder` source in the deployment whose `include`
matches `.pdf` files starts parsing them too, and so do deployments created
with `okg deployment bootstrap`, which writes the same file.

### No model calls by default

With the default `extractors.yaml` and embeddings off (the default), adding
and reading a folder of PDFs makes no model call: no captioning or
table-transcription client is built, no embedding service is called, and no
API key is needed. The three things that do call a model are opt-ins: a
`captioning` block, a table-transcription block, and embeddings. Add none of
them and nothing leaves the machine.

A test backs this. It runs the whole flow, from preview through publish and a
search, as child processes with the named model clients (LiteLLM, OpenAI,
Anthropic, OKG's captioning, vision and table clients) rigged to fail, and any
Python network connection that leaves the machine rigged to fail
(`test_adding_and_searching_a_pdf_folder_makes_no_model_calls` in
`tests/substrate/sources/test_guided_add_journeys.py`). A second test turns
captioning on to show the rigging fires. The test cannot see a model call made
by something other than Python in these processes.

## Files it cannot read

`add-source` reads Markdown (`.md`, `.markdown`), text (`.txt`, `.rst`), JSON
(`.json`), YAML (`.yaml`, `.yml`) and PDF (`.pdf`). A file with an unknown or
missing extension is read as JSON if its first bytes are `{` followed by a
newline, or `{"`. No other format is recognised from first bytes. Images are
read only when the deployment's `extractors.yaml` turns captioning on. A file
of any other type that your `include` patterns match, such as a Word file,
still becomes a record, but the record holds only the file name and nothing in
the file is searchable.

The preview and the apply result both count those files and print a warning
that names each type and how many files it covers. If none of the matched
files can be read, `add-source` refuses and tells you how to narrow `include`.
In the JSON output, the warning is in `warnings` (additive; empty when every
matched file is readable). On a refusal, `warnings` is empty and the same
counts are in the failed step: `steps[].detail.unreadable_files`. A PDF with
no text gets its own warning there, of kind `pdf_without_text`.

## Check it

```bash
okg search --deployment <name> --query '<a word from a file>'
```

A match is a `document` (a file, named `doc:notes:<path>`) or a
`document_chunk` (a passage of one). After you edit or delete a file, run
`okg ingest --deployment <name>`: a search then finds the new text, and a
deleted file's records are gone.

## When it fails

- `folder /path does not exist or is not a directory`: pass the folder's
  absolute path in `root=`.
- Any other failed step: see
  [If a step fails](index.md#connect-the-source).
